text: John Dixon Gibbs (14 July 1833–6 March 1912) was a British engineer and financier who, along with Lucien Gaulard, is commonly credited as the co-inventor of the AC step-down transformer. The transformer was first demonstrated in 1883 at London's Royal Aquarium; at the time, the term "transformer" had not been coined, and the device was referred to as a "secondary generator." Although Gibbs is often credited equally with Gaulard, his role appears to have been primarily that of a financial backer and businessman. He was one of the initial subscribers to the "National Company for Distribution of Electricity by Secondary Generators," registered on 11 May 1883, and attended the company's third ordinary annual general meeting in March 1886, delivering an address on its business progress. Despite the underlying physics—mainly Faraday's law of induction—being known since the 1830s, transformers became practical only after Gaulard and Gibbs introduced their design in 1883, which featured an iron core acting as a magnetic circuit. This design was initially seen as overcomplicated due to its movable armature; it attracted the attention of Sir Coutts Lindsay, who used it to power the Grosvenor Gallery, one of Britain's first lighting systems powered by a central generating station. In 1885, Ottó Bláthy, Miksa Déri, and Károly Zipernowsky secured a patent on a similar design using laminated metal sheets to reduce eddy currents. Information about an exhibition of Gibbs and Gaulard's transformer in Turin, Italy in 1884 was published in 1885 and drew the attention of George Westinghouse. In the summer of 1885, Westinghouse purchased the American rights to Gibbs and Gaulard's design and ordered several transformers from them to be shipped to his Pittsburgh factory. Westinghouse then commissioned engineer William Stanley, Jr. to design an electric lighting system using the transformers, leading to significant improvements in the design, for which Stanley is often credited instead. In July 1889, Gibbs was reported as one of the four initial directors of the newly registered British company "The Westinghouse Electric Co. Ltd." (George Westinghouse junior being another director). Gibbs had his work patented under German patent no. 28947, recognized in Great Britain, but the patent was disputed by Sebastian Ziani de Ferranti. Following patent litigation, Gibbs and Gaulard lost the patent; Gibbs appealed the case to the House of Lords, where he again lost, resulting in his financial ruin.
